Talk is Cheap, Communication is Hard: Dynamic Grounding Failures and Repair in Multi-Agent Negotiation

Yiheng Yao, Chelsea Zou, and Robert D. Hawkins

Stanford University

Preprint. Under review.

Keywords: multi-agent communication, grounding, negotiation, resource allocation, discourse pragmatics

 

Grounding is the collaborative process of establishing mutual belief sufficient for the current communicative purpose. While static grounding maps language to a shared, externally observable context, dynamic grounding is a joint activity where meaning is negotiated through interaction. Current multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) benchmarks focus on static, one-shot tasks, overlooking the ability to repair grounding breakdowns across turns. We introduce an iterated, multi-turn negotiation game in which two agents allocate shared resources toward private projects with verifiable jointly optimal outcomes. While individual agents can identify Pareto-optimal allocations in isolation, agent dyads consistently fail to reach them across open- and closed-source models. Our investigation reveals four failure modes: (1) coordination degrades when shared interaction history is absent; (2) yet accumulated context can itself become a liability through stubborn anchoring, where initial proposals are treated as axiomatic rather than negotiable; (3) a reliance on perfunctory fairness (equal resource splits) over reward-maximizing coordination; and (4) failures in referential binding, where agents lose track of commitments across turns. These results highlight dynamic grounding as a critical and understudied axis of multi-agent coordination. Our framework decomposes the coordination gap into measurable components: the oracle baseline establishes that the gap is not attributable to individual reasoning limitations; the no-talk baseline establishes that communication is necessary; and a full-transparency intervention establishes that information exchange alone is insufficient: the bottleneck lies in the interactive processes of joint plan formation, commitment, and execution that constitute dynamic grounding.

1. Introduction

Successful communication requires more than exchanging propositions; it requires grounding—the collaborative process by which interlocutors establish that their utterances have been understood well enough for current purposes (Clark & Brennan, 1991). In human dialogue, grounding is an active, incremental process: speakers monitor comprehension, request clarification, and repair misunderstandings in real time. This dynamic grounding stands in contrast to static grounding, which links language to a fixed, externally observable context such as a knowledge base or image (Chandu et al., 2021; Anikina et al., 2025).

Dynamic grounding is central to many real-world coordination problems. Consider project managers coordinating multiple workstreams under shared resource constraints: engineering hours, compute capacity, and testing bandwidth must be divided across concurrent projects, each with different requirements and deadlines. No single manager sees the full picture while each advocates for their own projects’ needs. Reaching an efficient allocation requires not just stating demands, but explaining why resources are needed, understanding competing priorities, and negotiating trade-offs through repeated planning meetings. As LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed to act autonomously on behalf of users, their ability to coordinate through this kind of multi-turn, goal-driven dialogue becomes critical.

Yet current multi-agent LLM benchmarks remain overwhelmingly focused on static tasks: matching descriptions to images (Eisenstein et al., 2026), optimizing fixed payoff matrices (Bianchi et al., 2024), or reaching agreement on predefined price points (Davidson et al., 2024). These paradigms test whether models can communicate facts, but not whether they can build and maintain shared understanding through interaction—the hallmark of dynamic grounding.

We argue that the gap between static and dynamic grounding is the key bottleneck for multi-agent LLM coordination. To study this, we introduce an iterated, multi-turn negotiation game in which two agents share a pool of resources and must allocate them toward private projects with different resource requirements and rewards (Figure 1). Within each round, agents engage in multi-turn cheap talk before making simultaneous purchase decisions; across rounds, they face the same or new partners and scenarios (projects to pursue), enabling the study of grounding accumulation, repair, and adaptation over multiple interactions. The asymmetric project structure creates an organic need for dynamic grounding. Agents must discuss not just what resources they want, but why—which projects they are pursuing, which resources are flexible, and how to coordinate to avoid costly overdraw penalties. Crucially, we design scenarios with verifiable joint optimal outcomes, enabling precise measurement of the gap between what agents could achieve and what they do achieve. Admittedly, it is difficult to directly observe shared understanding; rather, verifiable outcomes and interaction traces from our environment let us surface and diagnose where dynamic grounding breaks down.

Our experiments reveal individual agents can identify optimal strategies in isolation (oracle baseline), but interacting dyads consistently underperform. We trace this gap to four failure modes: (1) coordination degrades when shared interaction history is absent; (2) yet accumulated context can itself become a liability through stubborn anchoring, where initial proposals are treated as axiomatic rather than negotiable; (3) perfunctory fairness, where agents default to equal resource splits rather than coordinating on reward-maximizing allocations; and (4) referential binding failures, where agents lose track of prior commitments across turns.

Our contributions are: (i) a configurable negotiation game environment that isolates the costs of interactive coordination from individual reasoning capacity, with verifiable outcomes; (ii) an empirical decomposition of the coordination gap showing that the bottleneck lies in interactive plan formation and commitment (not reasoning limitations or information asymmetry), together with a characterization of four failure modes; and (iii) a framework for studying interventions including better prompt design, structured agent interaction patterns, and collecting game traces for offline training in the future.

2. Related work

Our work sits at the intersection of three lines of research: grounding in dialogue, LLM-based negotiation, and multi-agent coordination. We review each and identify the gap our framework addresses.

2.1 Grounding in dialogue

The concept of grounding originates in Clark & Brennan (1991), who define it as the process of establishing mutual belief sufficient for current purposes. In cognitive science, grounding encompasses both static symbol grounding—mapping language to perceptual or external referents—and dynamic communicative grounding, where shared understanding is built interactively over the common ground that interlocutors mutually presuppose (Stalnaker, 2002). NLP research has overwhelmingly focused on the former, neglecting the dynamic, interactive dimension (Chandu et al., 2021). A recent survey of 448 papers highlights that evaluation frameworks for dynamic grounding in Language Model (LM) interactions remain largely absent (Anikina et al., 2025). Our work targets this gap: we design a task that requires communication for success, where agents must negotiate shared plans, repair misunderstandings, and track commitments across turns to achieve optimal outcomes.

2.2 LLM-based negotiation

A growing literature evaluates LLMs in structured negotiation settings, spanning landlord–tenant bargaining with distributive and compatible issues (Davidson et al., 2024), six-agent multi-issue negotiations under cooperative, greedy, and adversarial dynamics (Abdelnabi et al., 2024), resource exchange and ultimatum games (Bianchi et al., 2024), game-theoretic equilibrium computation (Hua et al., 2024), and multi-party bargaining with hidden reward structures (Qian et al., 2026). Two patterns emerge across this work. First, while many games are multi-turn (agents exchange messages before a decision), they are rarely iterated: agents negotiate once over a fixed set of issues, with no opportunity for grounding repair across repeated encounters. Second, evaluation focuses on outcome metrics—deal rates, scores, Pareto efficiency—rather than on the communicative process. Our framework addresses both gaps: each round features multi-turn cheap talk followed by a simultaneous decision, and rounds are iterated with stable or shifting partners, enabling the study of grounding accumulation and repair.

2.3 Multi-agent coordination

MT-PingEval (Eisenstein et al., 2026) benchmarks collaborative private information games under a fixed token budget with variable turn counts, introducing a formal hierarchy of interactivity levels (see Appendix A for where our game falls). A key finding is that LLMs generally fail to improve with more interaction turns, producing content-rich utterances that they “struggle to deploy strategically in service of collaborative goals.” We extend this paradigm to an iterated setting to study whether agents can recover from such failures across repeated encounters.

The hidden profile paradigm (Stasser & Titus, 1985)—where optimal group decisions require pooling privately held information—has recently been applied to LLM agents in HiddenBench (Li et al., 2026), revealing a large performance gap between single agents with complete information and multi-agent groups that must pool asymmetric evidence through discussion. Our game introduces both compatible and conflicting goals, where information asymmetry arises naturally from private project assignments. Complementary work shows that even minimal communication (a single-word channel) can increase cooperation from 0% to 48.3% in a Stag Hunt (Madmoun, 2026), though such channels are insufficient for the richer referential grounding our task requires. Most recently, Khatua et al. (2026) document coordination failures in collaborative coding agent teams—including vague messages, commitment violations, and incorrect partner expectations—observing that dyadic performance falls 30% below solo baselines. Our work isolates the communicative acts underlying such failures in a controlled setting, enabling systematic study of when and why coordination breaks down.

3. Game environment

Two agents share a pool of resources (e.g., wood, stone, gold), each with a fixed per-round supply and unit cost. Each agent has an independent budget and simultaneously submits a purchase decision each round; if combined demand for any resource exceeds supply, the round is annulled and both agents receive zero reward. Rather than assigning scalar values to resources directly, each agent is assigned private projects: combinatorial goals requiring specific resource mixes and yielding rewards per completed run (e.g., 3 wood + 2 stone →\rightarrow 50 points). Unspent budget has no value. This project layer shifts the pragmatics from negotiating quantities to communicating why particular combinations matter, creating a natural need for referential grounding around project names, requirements, and strategies. Using the interactivity hierarchy of Eisenstein et al. (2026), we show in Appendix A that this structure makes the game at least level-3 interactive but not level-2 interactive; meaning that at least 3 messages need to be shared before the optimal joint allocation can be solved.

Each game consists of multiple rounds (set to 4 for our study). Within each round, agents first engage in cheap talk: up to 5 turns each of alternating natural-language messages, during which they may share project information, propose allocations, or negotiate. Each agent also maintains a private thinking scratchpad hidden from the opponent, enabling comparison of private intent with public speech. Agents then independently submit a resource allocation together with project assignments as structured json. After both decisions, the round resolves: overdraw is checked, rewards are computed, and both agents observe the opponent’s purchases. Opponent rewards are not disclosed unless voluntarily shared.

3.1 Scenario generation

We parameterize goal conflict via the compatibility ratio M/CM/C: the maximum achievable joint reward MM divided by the sum of individual maxima C=V1+V2C=V_{1}+V_{2} (each agent optimizing independently). When M/C=1.0M/C=1.0, optimal strategies are fully compatible; when M/C<1.0M/C<1.0, individual optima conflict. We generate scenarios at three levels: M/C∈{0.5,0.8,1.0}M/C\in\{0.5,0.8,1.0\}.

Scenarios are generated via simulated annealing. The generator initializes six random projects (three per agent), then iteratively perturbs requirements, rewards, and assignments to minimize a composite loss targeting the desired M/CM/C ratio (±0.05\pm 0.05). The loss jointly enforces: equal individual maxima (V1=V2V_{1}=V_{2}); swap fairness (the joint optimum can favor either agent equally); multiple joint-optimal solutions; and individual affordability of all projects. Thereafter, an oracle validation step further restricts the candidate pool to those that all models studied in subsequent games can solve under full information with a single attempt (pass@1) individually. This oracle baseline establishes that the coordination gap is not attributable to individual reasoning limitations—it isolates interaction itself as the locus of difficulty. The full list of scenarios is listed in Appendix C.

4. Experimental setup

We evaluate models spanning multiple providers: Claude 4.5 Sonnet (Anthropic), GPT-5 mini (OpenAI), and Qwen 3.5 Flash (via OpenRouter); see Appendix B for model configuration details. Prompt templates are provided in Appendix D. N=10N=10 games are played for each of 3×2×2=123\times 2\times 2=12 conditions, with all-to-all model cross-play (6 unique pairings) yielding a total of 720 game traces. Each game consists of 4 iterated rounds for a total of 2880 dyadic multi-turn interactions leading to a decision. All traces (cheap talk transcripts, thinking logs, allocations, rewards, and experiment metadata) are stored for reproducibility and released for further analysis; see Appendix G. To mitigate confounds, each configuration is played twice with first-speaker roles swapped, controlling for order effects, and abstract resource identifiers are replaced at runtime with a list of pre-sampled thematic names to amortize content biases (Appendix C).

4.1 Conditions and controls

  1. 1.

    Compatibility ratio (M/C∈{0.5,0.8,1.0}M/C\in\{0.5,0.8,1.0\}): varies the degree of goal conflict. Agents start without knowledge of the other parties’ projects and must communicate to determine whether their goals are aligned or opposed.

  2. 2.

    Partner stability: stable (same partner) vs. shifting (one agent’s context resets each round). This evaluates whether agents can leverage shared history to form ad-hoc conventions (Hawkins et al., 2023), a well-studied phenomenon in humans yet often overlooked in LLMs.

  3. 3.

    Project rotation: fixed vs. rotating (new scenarios each round). This holds the compatibility ratio constant, preserving the level of goal conflict, but eliminates a fixed environment and tests whether agents can develop transferable coordination strategies rather than memorizing prior successful allocations.

4.2 Metrics

We organize metrics into outcome metrics quantifying coordination quality and process metrics analyzing communicative strategies (Table 2).

5. Results

Table 3 summarizes coordination quality across models, pairings, and conditions. To decompose the coordination gap, we anchor results against three baselines: an oracle baseline (agents solving the allocation in isolation with full information) rules out individual reasoning limitations; a no-talk baseline (§5.1) establishes that communication is necessary; and a full-transparency intervention (§5.7) tests whether information asymmetry is the primary bottleneck. Within that frame, we isolate four behavioral failure modes (lack of shared interaction history, perfunctory fairness, anchoring, and referential binding failures) illustrated in Figure 6. Exploratory LLM-assisted trace annotations complement this picture in §6 (full taxonomy in Appendix I).

Across all conditions, 15.7% of rounds result in overdraw, concentrated in competitive scenarios (M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5: 24.7%) and rare in compatible ones (M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0: 6.9%). Despite this, most dyads eventually find effective coordination: 81.7% of games contain at least one jointly optimal round, and in the stable condition the first optimum is reached after an average of 1.6 rounds. After an overdraw, 83.3% of subsequent rounds yield positive scores, suggesting that coordination failures serve as effective learning signals.

Evaluating cross-play pairings reveals that heterogeneous dyads consistently outperform self-play under competitive conditions (Figure 2). At M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5, every cross-play pair exceeds the stronger model’s self-play baseline: Sonnet 4.5 ×\times GPT-5 Mini achieves 79.8% joint efficiency (vs. 68.2% and 63.7% self-play), GPT-5 Mini ×\times Qwen 3.5 reaches 74.0% (vs. 68.2%), and even Qwen 3.5 ×\times Sonnet 4.5 matches Sonnet’s self-play at 63.8%. This cross-play advantage under competition suggests that behavioral diversity aids coordination when goal conflict is high. The strongest synergy (Sonnet 4.5 ×\times GPT-5 Mini) may stem from complementary negotiation styles: Sonnet 4.5’s fairness appeals (§5.3) moderate GPT-5 Mini’s higher threat rate, yielding the lowest overdraw rates of any pairing (1.3% in compatible scenarios, 10.6% in competitive ones). As compatibility increases (M/C=0.8M/C{=}0.8 and 1.01.0), the cross-play advantage narrows and weaker models begin to drag down stronger partners. GPT-5 Mini ×\times Qwen 3.5 falls below GPT-5 Mini self-play at M/C=0.8M/C{=}0.8 (77.4% vs. 85.6%), suggesting that under reduced conflict, individual capability matters more than behavioral diversity.

5.1 The value of cheap talk

To quantify the contribution of communication, we compare dyads with multi-turn cheap talk against a no-talk baseline where agents submit allocations without any communication (Figure 3; full numeric breakdown in Table 9, Appendix F). The baseline is run as self-play only (N=4N{=}4 games per model ×\times partner-stability ×\times M/CM/C cell, yielding 32 rounds per cell).

Cheap talk produces large, consistent improvements across all models and conditions. Averaged across models and conditions, joint efficiency roughly triples under competition (M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5), rising from 18.0% to 63.2%. The gain persists under mixed (M/C=0.8M/C{=}0.8: 29.0% →\rightarrow 75.3%) and fully compatible goals (M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0: 56.8% →\rightarrow 87.2%). Even naturally aligned agents benefit substantially from communication, since multiple allocation plans may satisfy both agents’ individual optima and not all combinations are supply-compatible.

Supply violations tell a complementary story. Without communication, overdraw is pervasive at M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5: only 21.8% of rounds avoid a supply violation, meaning roughly four in five competitive no-talk rounds end in failure. Cheap talk lifts this to 69.5%, a 47.7-point gain. The gain remains large at M/C=0.8M/C{=}0.8 (33.0% →\rightarrow 81.2%, a 48.2-point jump) and M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 (61.5% →\rightarrow 91.2%, nearly 30 points). Optimum rates show the most dramatic lift: without communication, only 7.5% of competitive rounds reach the joint maximum, while cheap talk raises this to 33.0%; at M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0, optimum rates climb from 39.7% to 70.2%. These results confirm that in our experimental paradigm, cheap talk is indispensable to success.

5.2 Lack of shared interaction history

The shifting condition, where one agent’s context resets each round, degrades coordination for most models (Figure 4). The proportion of rounds achieving the joint optimum drops by 7.7 percentage points for Qwen 3.5 Flash and 6.3 points for GPT-5 Mini (averaged across M/C ratios; Table 9, Appendix F), consistent with accumulated history enabling grounding repair. Yet anchoring analysis reveals that accumulated context can also become a liability: among suboptimal non-overdrawn rounds at M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 where improvement was possible, Qwen’s stable dyads repeat their prior allocation in 60.8% of cases (31/51) compared to 20.8% in shifting (5/24). Though the shifting sample is small, the direction is consistent with the hypothesis that context resets break anchoring traps. Under fully compatible goals, Qwen locks into early suboptimal splits and fails to renegotiate, while forced re-negotiation in shifting inadvertently enables better outcomes.

Sonnet 4.5 is the exception, achieving slightly higher optimum rates in the shifting condition. Qwen 3.5 presents a striking anomaly at M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0: shifting substantially outperforms stable, reversing the expected pattern (Figure 4). This resilience is partly explained by differences in propensity for sustained communication during cheap talk (Figure 5). GPT-5 Mini and Qwen 3.5 Flash exhibit high early decision rates, submitting a resource allocation before the 5-turn conversation limit is reached. In contrast, Sonnet 4.5 exhibits a significantly lower early decision rate, more often fully exhausting conversational turns. This prolonged engagement facilitates dynamic grounding, allowing agent dyads with Sonnet 4.5 to maintain or even improve performance with new partners each round.

5.3 Strategy taxonomy

We classify negotiation behaviors using rule-based extraction (Appendix E). Table 4 reports per-model rates at the agent-round level, attributing each utterance to the speaker. Other-directed proposals (“you take NN of XX”) are infrequent overall (9.9%), with Sonnet 4.5 proposing most often (13.4%) and GPT-5 Mini least (6.5%). The most striking differences are rhetorical: Sonnet 4.5 appeals to fairness in 52.9% of its utterances (74.8% under competition), while GPT-5 Mini is the most threatening model (14.1%, peaking at 20.6% under M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5). Qwen 3.5 Flash rarely threatens (5.6%) and appeals to fairness least (35.9%). While all models concentrate these strategies in competitive scenarios, sharp differences in magnitude suggest distinct, persistent “negotiation personalities.” Payoff alternation, where the higher-reward agent flips between consecutive rounds, is rare (16.3% of pairs), and sustained 4-round alternation, a rationally optimal coordination strategy, is almost nonexistent (2.2%). Agents exhibit strong lose-shift (84.3%) and moderate win-stay (51.5%) behavior.

5.4 Perfunctory fairness

We detect equal splits—rounds where both agents request identical quantities of a shared resource—in 12.5% of rounds. Of these, 48.8% co-occur with suboptimal outcomes, yielding an overall perfunctory fairness rate of 6.1%. This pattern reflects a coordination shortcut: agents default to an equal division that is safe but ignores the asymmetric project structure that makes unequal allocations jointly better. Models differ in their reliance on this heuristic: Sonnet 4.5 produces equal splits most frequently (15.9%, perfunctory fairness rate 7.3%), Qwen 3.5 Flash at an intermediate rate (12.7%, 6.7%), and GPT-5 Mini least (10.7%, 4.7%). The pattern suggests agents are satisficing on surface-level fairness rather than engaging in the deeper information exchange needed to discover what each agent actually requires. Rather than asking which resources are flexible or what projects are being pursued, agents default to equal division as a socially acceptable shortcut that avoids the conversational work of grounding asymmetric needs.

5.5 Anchoring and proposal deference

Stubborn anchoring

In games with the same scenario, agents repeat their exact joint allocation in 46.5% of rounds. The repeat rate is 55.1% following non-overdrawn rounds and 0.6% after overdraw, indicating that agents recognize and correct clear mistakes. However, repeating an allocation is not always optimal: of the 339 rounds that were suboptimal and non-overdrawn (i.e. failures the dyad could have corrected), 29.2% repeat the same allocation unchanged. This stubborn anchoring is more prevalent in stable games (40.7%) than shifting games (15.9%), where context resets discourage direct reuse, and increases with collaborative pressure: M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 games exhibit a 46.0% stubborn-anchor rate versus 28.3% at M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5, suggesting that in compatible situations, agents have less incentive to improve upon a prior suboptimal allocation.

First-proposal deference

Explicit other-directed proposals (“you take NN of resource XX”) appear in 12.9% of rounds, typically issued at the very first cheap-talk turn (median turn 1) before any information has been exchanged. In round 1 of non-rotating games, before either agent has observed an allocation outcome, 20.4% of these proposals are followed exactly. This uninformed compliance is costly: accepted proposals lead to suboptimal outcomes almost as often as optimal ones (8.2% vs. 12.2%). Across all rounds, deference is more prevalent when scenarios change: in non-rotating games, 15.5% of exact-match deferences produce suboptimal outcomes versus 16.9% optimal, and the imbalance worsens in rotating games (20.9% suboptimal vs. 14.4% optimal) where per-round scenario changes make early proposals especially uninformed. Models differ in compliance: Sonnet 4.5 accepts 44% of proposals, Qwen 3.5 Flash 32%, and GPT-5 Mini 21%. We read this as over-reliance on communicative satisficing rather than an outright grounding failure: consistent with Clark’s principle of least collaborative effort (Clark, 1996), accepting a “good enough” first proposal is a familiar human heuristic that conserves conversational effort and avoids social friction. In our task, however, the strategy is miscalibrated, as agents accept proposals before enough information has been exchanged to assess mutual benefit, and the shortcut locks dyads into suboptimal outcomes more often than not.

5.6 Referential binding failures

Of the 15.7% of rounds that result in overdraw, our heuristic pipeline (Appendix E) identifies positive agreement language in the final cheap-talk turns in 52.3%, cases where agents verbally committed to a split and then violated it at submission (stated-vs-actual coherence, Table 2). Manual inspection reveals two recurring subtypes (see Appendix H for annotated transcripts). In proposer amnesia, the agent that originated a split fails to honor it: its thinking trace re-derives a new allocation from scratch with no reference to its own prior proposal. In self-commitment abandonment, an agent proposes a plan, the opponent accepts, and the proposer reverts to an individual-maximizing allocation once a higher-reward option becomes salient, resembling the stylistic sycophancy of Eisenstein et al. (2026), where agreement language functions as social lubrication without updating the action plan. Agreements established in cheap talk appear not to be reliably retrieved as action constraints at decision time, resulting in a loss of common ground. We posit this failure results from the model failing to bind resource symbols to their earlier respective commitments.

Referential binding is the cognitive process of mapping a linguistic expression to a specific discourse referent. In the context of joint action (Clark, 1996), this mapping serves as a coordination device: once an agent confirms “I’ll take stone×\times6,” that quantity is anchored as a pragmatic constraint on its subsequent action. Mechanistic interpretability work has studied how LMs retrieve bound entities in context (Gur-Arieh et al., 2025), but only with simple single-query settings (“Pete loves jam, Ann loves pie. Who loves pie?”). Negotiation demands binding multiple entities simultaneously: strategies to resource-quantity pairs, quantities to agents, and prior commitments to action constraints, across a multi-turn dialogue interleaved with persuasion and counter-proposals. The failures we observe suggest that agreements established in cheap talk were not retrieved as constraints for the downstream action, resulting in the loss of common ground. Extending mechanistic binding analyses to such multi-entity, multi-turn settings is a promising direction for future research.

5.7 Full-transparency intervention

To isolate how much of the coordination gap stems from information asymmetry, we ran a full-transparency intervention in which both agents’ complete project specifications are revealed in the system prompt before cheap talk begins, eliminating information asymmetry entirely. We selected the Qwen 3.5 Flash ×\times GPT-5 Mini pair for this intervention: it is the weakest-performing cross-play pair at M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5 (74.0% efficiency, Table 3), and GPT-5 Mini shows the highest Specification Dispute rate of any model in our judge analysis (52.3% of its suboptimal rounds, §6), making it the most conservative test of whether information asymmetry is the primary bottleneck. We ran N=120N{=}120 games across all three compatibility ratios, both partner-stability conditions, and both project-rotation conditions.

Full transparency consistently reduced overdraw (12.3% →\rightarrow 8.1%, Δ=−4.2\Delta{=}{-}4.2 pp) and raised joint efficiency (79.6% →\rightarrow 85.3%, Δ=+5.7\Delta{=}{+}5.7 pp), with the sharpest gains in the stable competitive condition (M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5: overdraw 11.2%→3.8%11.2\%~\rightarrow~3.8\%, efficiency 78.1%→89.0%78.1\%~\rightarrow~89.0\%). However, the optimum rate showed no reliable improvement overall (55.6% →\rightarrow 53.1%) and even declined at M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 (69.4% →\rightarrow 64.4%), where project requirements are already non-conflicting.

Our static process metrics distinguish which failure modes are ameliorated by shared information from those rooted in the interactive process itself. Perfunctory fairness is nearly eliminated (5.0% →\rightarrow 1.7%): when both agents can see the asymmetric project structure directly, the equal-split shortcut is visibly costly, removing the incentive for the effort-minimizing heuristic. Stubborn anchoring, by contrast, more than doubles (23.1% →\rightarrow 46.7%), suggesting the failure is driven by commitment dynamics rather than uncertainty about the partner’s needs. With full information established upfront, agents converge on an early plan and then do not renegotiate even when the allocation is suboptimal. The stable/shifting optimum gap also reverses sign under transparency, though this should be interpreted cautiously given Qwen 3.5 Flash’s known anomalous behavior in the stable M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 condition (Figure 4). A smaller joint-transparency variant (N=12N{=}12) that additionally exposed each agent’s reward function achieved the highest optimum rate observed (64.6%), suggesting that knowing the opponent’s incentives, not just resource needs, matters for closing the residual gap.

These results establish that the coordination bottleneck is not reducible to information asymmetry. Full per-condition outcome metrics are in Table 8 (Appendix F); exploratory LLM judge pattern comparisons between baseline and transparency conditions are in Table 15 (Appendix I).

6. Discussion

Together, our three baselines decompose the coordination gap and localize the bottleneck. The oracle baseline rules out individual reasoning limitations: agents can identify optimal allocations in isolation, so the gap is not attributable to bounded rationality. The no-talk baseline establishes that communication is necessary: without cheap talk, joint efficiency roughly triples under competition (§5.1), confirming that information exchange is a prerequisite for coordination. The full-transparency intervention (§5.7) then isolates what shared information can and cannot fix. Transparency reduces overdraw and dissolves perfunctory fairness, confirming those are partly attributable to uncertainty about the partner’s portfolio. The optimum rate, however, does not reliably improve, and stubborn anchoring intensifies. The failures that persist under full information, namely anchoring, commitment-action decoupling, and referential binding, are therefore not reducible to information asymmetry. They are grounded in the interactive process itself: joint plan formation, commitment maintenance, and execution under cheap talk. The grounding gap is not a gap in knowledge or reasoning capacity; it is a gap in the ability to coordinate action across turns.

Connection to grounding theory

Our failure modes map onto established mechanisms. Anchoring reflects a breakdown of Clark and Brennan’s contribution–acceptance cycle (Clark & Brennan, 1991): proposals enter common ground without verification, and in Traum’s terms (Traum, 1994), agents over-initiate while under-acknowledging. First offers pull final outcomes even in LLM negotiations (Tversky & Kahneman, 1974; Takenami et al., 2025), and this resembles sycophancy (Perez et al., 2023; Sharma et al., 2024); while Eisenstein et al. (2026) found agents can reject incorrect proposals in their chess task, our agents fail to establish the mutual information sufficient for the task at hand. Perfunctory fairness reflects minimizing individual rather than joint effort (Clark & Wilkes-Gibbs, 1986), and the win-stay/lose-shift pattern mirrors the Pavlov strategy (Nowak & Sigmund, 1993), effective reactively but unable to improve on suboptimal successes.

LLM-assisted behavioral analysis

To more granularly examine agent communication patterns at scale, we ran an LLM-as-judge pipeline over all 720 game traces (details in Appendix I).

The resulting taxonomy is summarised in the inset; full prevalence rates and canonical examples appear in Appendix I. The negative patterns cluster around the grounding failure modes identified in §5: Specification Dispute (31.2% of suboptimal rounds) captures incompatible mental models; Agreement Abandonment (15.3%) captures commitment failures; Defensive Underbidding (17.6%) and Greedy Monopolization (14.0%) capture the two faces of anchoring. On the positive side, Complementary Partitioning (33.4% of optimal rounds), Precedent Replication (28.5%), and Explicit Quantity Confirmation (26.6%) reflect successful grounding acts. The appendix further documents model-dependent idiosyncrasies in pattern prevalence (Appendix I). The reported prevalence rates should be interpreted as directional indicators rather than precise measurements: the judge pipeline has not been validated against human annotations, and the quantitative values are subject to label noise from the automated taxonomy consolidation step.

Limitations & Future Work

Our study is limited to dyadic, text-only interactions between three small models; flagship models and human-agent dyads remain untested. While our project structure adds complexity over scalar payoff matrices, it remains a stylized abstraction. Specifically, our environment assumes symmetric power dynamics and enforces a fixed 5-turn communication window, whereas real-world grounding frequently involves hierarchical leverage and open-ended dialogue. Our process metrics combine rule-based regex classification with an LLM judge pipeline, but both lack a human-annotated baseline for validation; robustly establishing the accuracy of the LLM judge against human judgement remains an open step. Further isolating grounding breakdowns from rational defection, and expanding this framework to multi-party coalitions (N>2N>2) or environments with strategic perturbations (e.g., agents with adversarial personas), remain critical frontiers for future work.

Our failure mode analysis surfaces targeted directions for future intervention work. Overdraw reflects a commitment–action decoupling: agents reach verbal agreement but submit inconsistent allocations. Structured grounding protocols (e.g., requiring agents to echo the agreed split in their final action, or adding a lightweight post-negotiation verification step) directly address this failure. Failed improvement reveals that dyads frequently stabilize on suboptimal equilibria; training or prompting agents to explore more diverse solution pathways, rather than anchoring to prior allocations, could break this fixation. Perfunctory fairness is less about equity and more about a low-effort heuristic that short-circuits the search for more optimal solutions: equal splits require minimal reasoning and arise even when complementary splits would be strictly better for both parties; richer structured information exchange, as demonstrated by our transparency intervention, largely dissolves this pattern. Finally, our shifting-vs.-stable comparison reveals that a consistent partner is helpful for coordination: efficiency is systematically higher in stable dyads, suggesting that agent architectures equipped with persistent partner models or episodic interaction summaries would materially reduce grounding failures in multi-session deployments.

7. Conclusion

We introduced an iterated negotiation game that decomposes the coordination gap into measurable components. The oracle baseline establishes that the gap is not attributable to individual reasoning limitations. The no-talk baseline establishes that communication is necessary. Our full-transparency intervention establishes that information exchange alone is insufficient—the bottleneck lies in the interactive processes of joint plan formation, commitment, and execution that constitute dynamic grounding. This decomposition clarifies the target for intervention: structured grounding protocols, commitment scaffolding, and persistent partner models address the residual gap that neither better reasoning nor more information can close. As LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents, the ability to dynamically ground and align intents and goals across multiple interactions remains an essential, understudied capability for agentic deployment.

Claude Code (Anthropic) was used as a coding assistant for game engine development, data processing scripts, and the generation of appendix sections (strategy taxonomy operationalization, scenario listings, and prompt templates). Perplexity, Gemini, and Claude were used for synthesis during literature review. All outputs were reviewed and edited by the authors. The experimental results, analysis, and scientific conclusions are the authors’ own.

Appendix A Interactivity level analysis

Eisenstein et al. (2026) propose a formal hierarchy of interactivity levels for collaborative games with private information, where level kk indicates that kk messages must be exchanged before a player can produce a correct answer. Their framework assumes a shared objective; we use it to establish a lower bound on the communication required in our game, where agents are instructed to maximize their own individual reward.

Let X1X_{1} and X2X_{2} denote each agent’s private project information. Both agents must submit allocation decisions. We claim our game is at least level-3 interactive assuming the players are initially unaware of the M/CM/C ratio (degree of goal compatibility):

  1. 1.

    Agent 2 shares their project requirements: f2​(X2)f_{2}(X_{2}).

  2. 2.

    Agent 1, now informed of both sets of projects, computes and proposes a specific compatible allocation: f1​(X1,S2)f_{1}(X_{1},S_{2}).

  3. 3.

    Agent 2 verifies the proposal against their own projects and confirms or counter-proposes: f2​(X2,S1)f_{2}(X_{2},S_{1}).

This third turn is necessary regardless of the compatibility ratio. Even when M/C=1.0M/C=1.0, multiple allocation plans may satisfy both agents’ individual optima, and not all combinations are supply-compatible—without explicit coordination on which plan to execute, overdraw can occur. When M/C<1.0M/C<1.0, the candidate plans additionally involve trade-offs between agents’ rewards, making the confirmation step more contentious.

These three turns represent only the information-exchange minimum. Since agents maximize individual rewards, an additional bargaining dimension arises that the interactivity framework does not capture: agents must negotiate over who concedes what, a process whose difficulty scales with goal incompatibility. The information-exchange minimum (level 3) is constant across compatibility conditions; the compatibility ratio modulates the difficulty of the bargaining problem that follows.

Appendix B LLM model configuration details

Table 5 summarizes the API configuration for each model used in our experiments. All models use streaming responses. A 1-second cooldown is enforced between consecutive API calls, with up to 10 retries using exponential backoff (base 2s, max 120s) for rate-limit errors. Malformed JSON responses are retried up to 3 times per decision.

Agent errors

Across 950 games (3,800 rounds), 29.4% of games contain at least one logged error event (496 total; 0.52 per game). Importantly, validation_error and output_format_warning events (436 combined, 87.9%) are retriable: the engine re-prompts the agent up to 3 times before escalating. A heuristic_fallback entry is the definitive signal that an agent failed to produce a valid allocation after all retries—only 20 such events occur in the dataset, all from Qwen 3.6 Plus (an exploratory model outside the main reported set), attributable to sustained rate-limit failures exhausting the retry budget. decision_auto_filled (20 events, also Qwen 3.6 Plus) indicates rounds where a default zero-allocation was substituted as a result. Rounds containing heuristic fallbacks are excluded from all analyses. All three main models (Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5 Mini, Qwen 3.5 Flash) recovered within the retry budget on every round; their per-round error rates reflect only retriable validation errors: Qwen 3.5 Flash 0.073, Sonnet 4.5 0.071, GPT-5 Mini 0.047. The two exploratory models show higher rates: MiniMax M2.7 0.090 (validation errors only) and Qwen 3.6 Plus 0.048 (inclusive of the rate-limit fallbacks).

GPT-5 Mini and GPT-5.4 Mini use OpenAI’s max_completion_tokens parameter and do not support explicit temperature settings. All other models use the standard max_tokens parameter with temperature 0.7. Anthropic models support prompt caching; reasoning content (chain-of-thought) is extracted and stored separately from speech for all models that produce it.

Appendix D Detailed game prompts

This appendix provides the complete prompt templates used in our negotiation game. All prompts are defined in backend/agents/prompts.py and dynamically instantiated based on game configuration. We present prompts for the project-based reward system (schema version 5+), which is used for all experiments reported in the main text.

D.1 System prompt structure

Each agent receives a system-level prompt at the start of the game that remains constant throughout all rounds. The prompt consists of four main sections: game rules, project specifications, response format, and strategic context.

D.1.1 Game rules

## Game Rules - Resources available: {resource_types} - Resource supply per round: {resource_supply} - Resource costs: {resource_costs} - Your budget per round: ${agent_budget} - You may purchase at most {max_types} different resource types per round. - Resources do NOT carry over between rounds — each round starts fresh with a new budget and new supply. - If total demand for ANY resource exceeds supply, the round is ANNULLED and both parties get 0 reward.

Example instantiation (stable, collaborative condition):

- Resources available: wood, stone, gold - Resource supply per round: {"wood": 10, "stone": 10, "gold": 6} - Resource costs: {"wood": 1, "stone": 1.5, "gold": 3} - Your budget per round: $15 - You may purchase at most 2 different resource types per round.

D.1.2 Project specifications

## Projects You have 3 projects. Each project requires specific resources per run and yields a reward per run. The other party has their own projects with different requirements and rewards. Your reward = sum of (runs × reward) for each project you can complete with your purchased resources. IMPORTANT: Unspent money has NO value — only completed project runs count towards your score. NOTE: If you purchase resources but lack the full set required to complete at least one run of any project, your reward is 0 (this is NOT an annulment — the round proceeds normally, you simply completed no projects). {projects_info} {opponent_projects_info}

Example instantiation (agent with complementary projects):

- project_a: requires [stone×2], reward = 6/run - project_b: requires [wood×5, gold×3], reward = 15/run - project_c: requires [stone×4], reward = 10/run

D.1.3 Decision format

## Decision Format Submit a JSON object with your resource purchases AND project allocations: {"wood": 3, "gold": 1, "projects": {"project_a": 1, "project_b": 2}} The "projects" field specifies how many times to run each project. If omitted, the engine assigns resources to projects automatically by prioritizing projects in the order presented to you.

D.1.4 Response format (thinking enabled)

For agents with private thinking scratchpads (all experiments in main text):

## Response Format You MUST always respond with a JSON object containing exactly three fields: { "thinking": "your private reasoning (hidden from the other party)", "speech": "your message to the other party (visible to them)", "action": null } - Set "action" to null while you want to keep chatting. - Set "action" to a purchase object with project allocation to finalize. - "speech" MUST NOT be empty — always say something to the other party. Example — chatting: {"thinking": "They might want gold. I should bluff.", "speech": "I’m thinking about gold. What about you?", "action": null} Example — purchasing: {"thinking": "I’ll buy wood for my projects.", "speech": "Good luck!", "action": {"wood": 5, "stone": 2, "projects": {"project_a": 1, "project_b": 1}}} IMPORTANT: Respond with ONLY the JSON object. No text before or after it. I will guide you through each phase with instructions.

For Anthropic models, an additional suffix is appended to enforce JSON compliance:

IMPORTANT: You MUST respond with ONLY a valid JSON object. No other text before or after. The JSON must have exactly three fields: ’thinking’ (string), ’speech’ (string), and ’action’ (null or object).

D.1.5 Strategic context

The final section varies by experimental condition:

Stable partners (default):

## Your Situation - Your goal: maximize your cumulative reward across all rounds - The other party is also purchasing from the same shared pool.

Shifting partners (partner context resets each round):

## Your Situation - Your goal: maximize your cumulative reward across all rounds - You are playing against a DIFFERENT opponent each round.

Project sharing condition (intervention):

IMPORTANT — As a FIRST step in each round’s cheap talk, share your project details (names, resource requirements, rewards) with the other party and ask them to share theirs.

Theory-of-mind condition (intervention):

IMPORTANT — During each round’s cheap talk, actively reason about the other party’s goals and which projects they might be trying to run. Consider what resources they need, how their interests align or conflict with yours, and how you can use this understanding to inform your strategy.

Additionally, in the Theory-of-mind condition, the following reminder is appended to the Turn 0 cheap talk prompt:

Reminder: Actively reason about the other party’s goals and which projects they might be trying to run. Consider what resources they need and how their interests align or conflict with yours.

D.2 User prompts: cheap talk phase

After the system prompt, agents receive user-level prompts that guide them through each phase of the game. The cheap talk phase uses alternating prompts based on turn number.

D.2.1 Initial cheap talk prompt (Turn 0)

--- CHEAP TALK PHASE (Round {round_number}/{num_rounds}) --- Exchange messages with the other party ({turns_info}). Respond with JSON. Set "action" to null to keep chatting, or to a purchase object to finalize. [If opponent spoke first:] The other party said: "{opponent_message}"

Where turns_info is either “up to 5 exchanges this round” (default) or “as much as required” if cheap_talk_turns=0.

Example for Round 1 of 4-round game:

--- CHEAP TALK PHASE (Round 1/4) --- Exchange messages with the other party (up to 5 exchanges this round). Respond with JSON. Set "action" to null to keep chatting, or to a purchase object to finalize.

D.2.2 Subsequent cheap talk prompts (Turn >> 0)

The other party said: "{opponent_message}" Respond with JSON.

Example:

The other party said: "Hello! I’m considering wood and stone primarily. What are you leaning towards?" Respond with JSON.

D.2.3 Rotating projects notification (Rounds >> 1)

When project_rotation=True, agents receive new project assignments each round. The turn 0 prompt for subsequent rounds is prepended with:

NEW PROJECTS FOR THIS ROUND: - {project_name}: requires [{requirements}], reward = {reward}/run ... [Regular cheap talk prompt follows]

D.3 User prompts: decision phase

If agents have not submitted early during cheap talk, they receive a forced decision prompt after exhausting the turn limit.

--- DECISION PHASE --- Now submit your resource purchases and project allocations. Choose at most {max_types} resource types. Total cost must not exceed ${budget}. Respond with JSON. You MUST set "action" to your purchase object (include "projects" to specify runs).

Example:

--- DECISION PHASE --- Now submit your resource purchases and project allocations. Choose at most 2 resource types. Total cost must not exceed $15. Respond with JSON. You MUST set "action" to your purchase object (include "projects" to specify runs).

D.4 Round result notifications

After both agents submit decisions, they receive a notification with round outcomes.

D.4.1 Standard outcome notification message

--- Round result: You purchased {own_allocation}, ran projects [{project_runs}], and earned reward = {own_reward}. Opponent purchased {opponent_allocation}. ---

D.4.2 Annulled round (overdraw)

--- Round result: ANNULLED (total demand exceeded supply). Both parties receive 0 reward. Your bid: {own_allocation}. Opponent bid: {opponent_allocation}. ---

D.4.3 Project failure (no viable runs)

--- Round result: You purchased {own_allocation}, but could not complete any project runs (insufficient resources for any project), reward = 0. Opponent bid: {opponent_allocation}. ---

D.5 Post-game reflection prompt

After all rounds complete, LLM agents receive a reflection prompt to extract learnings. This leverages cached tokens from the full conversation history.

--- GAME COMPLETE ({total_rounds} rounds) --- Your cumulative reward: {own_cumulative_reward}. Opponent’s cumulative reward: {opponent_cumulative_reward}. Joint total: {joint_actual}. Theoretical joint maximum (optimal collaboration): {theoretical_max}. Efficiency achieved: {efficiency_pct}%. Reflect on the game and summarize key learnings that could help you achieve better outcomes in future games. Consider: - What strategies worked well or poorly? - How effective was your communication and negotiation approach? - What would you do differently next time? - Any patterns you noticed in resource allocation or opponent behavior? - How close did you get to the theoretical optimum? Provide a concise reflection (2-4 sentences) focusing on actionable insights.

Example:

--- GAME COMPLETE (4 rounds) --- Your cumulative reward: 48. Opponent’s cumulative reward: 52. Joint total: 100. Theoretical joint maximum (optimal collaboration): 140. Efficiency achieved: 71.4%. [Reflection prompt follows...]

D.6 No-thinking response format

For control conditions where agents have no private thinking channel (thinking=False), the response format section is replaced with:

## Response Format Everything you say is passed VERBATIM to the other party — you have NO private channel. The other party sees your FULL response. Think carefully about what you reveal. To send a message, respond with plain natural language text — NOT JSON, NOT a wrapper object. Just write your message directly as plain text. To finalize a purchase, respond with ONLY a JSON object with your resource purchases and project allocations: {"wood": 3, "gold": 1, "projects": {"project_a": 1, "project_b": 1}} I will guide you through each phase with instructions.

In this mode, cheap talk prompts do not request JSON responses:

--- CHEAP TALK PHASE (Round 1/4) --- Exchange messages with the other party (up to 5 exchanges this round). Send your opening message. Or end the round early by responding with ONLY a JSON purchase.

D.7 No-talk baseline prompt construction

The no-talk baseline (§5.1) sets enable_cheap_talk=False in the engine configuration. This elides the entire cheap-talk phase; agents proceed directly to the decision phase each round. The system prompt and decision-phase prompt are identical to the standard condition. Three components are omitted or modified relative to the talk condition:

  1. 1.

    Cheap talk prompts entirely elided. No --- CHEAP TALK PHASE --- messages are injected; agents never receive an opportunity to exchange natural-language messages.

  2. 2.

    Project updates injected directly before the decision prompt. In rotating-project games, new project assignments would normally arrive at the top of the cheap-talk turn 0 prompt. In no-talk mode these are appended directly to the agent’s context immediately before the --- DECISION PHASE --- prompt, preserving equivalent information access.

  3. 3.

    Post-game reflection elided. The reflection prompt (§D.5) is skipped; without a negotiation transcript there is no conversational history for the agent to reflect on.

The round-result notification (§D.4) is unchanged: agents still observe their own reward and the opponent’s allocation after each decision, providing the same outcome signal as in the talk condition.

D.8 Prompt instantiation details

Prompts are assembled dynamically by phase-specific functions in backend/agents/prompts.py (build_system_prompt(), cheap_talk_prompt(), decision_prompt(), round_result_message(), reflection_prompt()). Key implementation notes:

  • •

    Project names: Extracted from scenario generation, typically project_a, project_b, project_c. Decision examples use actual project names to aid grounding.

  • •

    Resource theming: Prompts receive themed resource names at instantiation time.

  • •

    Shifting mode redaction: In shifting mode, agent B sees only the current round; prompts hide multi-round context (“resources do NOT carry over” is removed as irrelevant).

  • •

    Turn limits: When cheap_talk_turns=0, prompts say “as many messages as necessary” rather than “up to 5 exchanges.” The decision phase is only triggered if an agent submits early; otherwise cheap talk continues indefinitely until both agents decide.

All prompt templates are version-controlled and experiment metadata records git commit hashes for full reproducibility (see Appendix B).

Abstract resource identifiers are replaced with thematic names sampled randomly at game initialization; the complete theme catalog is listed in Appendix C (Table 6). Project names remain abstract (project_a, project_b, project_c) regardless of theme, ensuring that semantic associations do not provide unintended hints about resource requirements or strategic value.

Appendix E Strategy taxonomy: operationalization

We classify negotiation strategies into six categories using deterministic, rule-based extraction applied to cheap-talk transcripts. All metrics are computed per round and aggregated per game. Below we define each metric and its extraction procedure.

1. Numeric sharing (self-proposal).

A round is marked as containing a self-proposal if either agent’s speech includes a first-person verb phrase followed by a numeric quantity and a resource name. The regex requires first-person framing to distinguish stated plans from descriptive mentions (e.g., “there are 10 wood available” does not match). Matched patterns include:

  • •

    (I’ll|I will|I plan to|I’m going to|...) (take|buy|get|...) \d+ <resource>

  • •

    my <resource>:\d+

  • •

    First-person focus verb + resource + quantity in the same clause

All speech messages from both agents are scanned (not just the first). A round scores 1 if any agent makes at least one numeric self-proposal. Rate: 48.8% of rounds.

2. Proposal for opponent (other-proposal).

Detected via “you”-framed verb phrases: you (take|get|buy|...) \d+ <resource>, as well as (leave|give|allocate) you \d+ <resource>. Only the first proposer’s message is considered. Rate: 12.7%.

3. Fairness appeal.

A round is marked positive if any agent’s speech contains one or more of the following terms (case-insensitive, word-boundary matched):

fair(ly|ness)?, equal(ly)?, split, half, 50/50, even(ly)?, both benefit, mutual(ly)?, equitabl(e|y), compromise, balance(d)?

Rate: 55.5% of rounds.

4. Threat.

Analogous keyword detection for adversarial language:

waste, punish, nothing, zero, take everything, all of it, overdraw, annul, block(ing)?, refuse, won’t cooperate, consequences, penalize, retaliat(e|ion), hurt

Rate: 19.2% of rounds.

5. Payoff alternation.

Computed for non-rotating games only (same scenario across rounds). For each consecutive pair of rounds (t,t+1)(t,t{+}1), we record whether the higher-reward agent flips: 𝟙[(rtA>rtB)≠(rt+1A>rt+1B)]\mathbb{1}[(r^{A}_{t}>r^{B}_{t})\neq(r^{A}_{t+1}>r^{B}_{t+1})]. The 2-round rate is the mean flip rate across all consecutive pairs per game. The 4-round rate requires full alternation over four consecutive rounds (wt≠wt+1≠wt+2≠wt+3w_{t}\neq w_{t+1}\neq w_{t+2}\neq w_{t+3}). 2-round rate: 16.8%; 4-round rate: 3.3%.

6. Win-stay / lose-shift.

Derived from the allocation anchoring analysis (consecutive-round allocation persistence in non-rotating games). Win-stay: the exact-match rate between consecutive joint allocations when the previous round was not overdrawn. Lose-shift: 1−exact_match1-\text{exact\_match} when the previous round was not jointly optimal (i.e. overdrawn or suboptimal). This broader “lose” definition captures rounds where the dyad succeeded but left joint reward on the table. Win-stay: 51.5%; Lose-shift: 84.3%.

7. Project information disclosure.

A speech turn is marked as disclosing private project information if it matches any of the following regex patterns (V5+ games only; V1–V4 use analogous value-function patterns):

  • •

    Project requirements: (project|plan)\w* (requires?|needs?|costs?|uses?) .*<resource>

  • •

    Project ownership: (my|i) (have|need|want) .*(project|plan)

  • •

    Resource-for-project: <resource>.*(for|to run|to complete) (my )?(project|plan)

  • •

    Project reward: (project|plan)\w* (gives?|pays?|yields?) \d+

  • •

    Reward per run: \d+ (points?|reward) (per|each|for) (run|completion|project)

  • •

    Active project work: (my|i) (am|’m) (working on|running|completing) (project|plan)

  • •

    Specific requirement: (i|my) (need|require|use) \d+ <resource> (per|each|for)

  • •

    Per-run cost: (each|per|one) (run|copy) of (my )?(project|plan) (needs?|requires?)

A round is marked positive if any agent speech turn in that round matches. Rate: 15.5% of rounds in the main cohort (720 games, main experiment run IDs).

8. Positive agreement language (referential binding heuristic).

Used to identify binding failure candidates: overdrawn rounds where positive commitment language appears in the final cheap-talk turns, suggesting the agents verbally agreed on a split before submitting an allocation that violated it. Detection applies a word-boundary regex to the last kk agent turns (default k=2k{=}2):

agree[sd]?, agreed, deal, sounds good, perfect, confirm(ed)?,
I(’ll| will) take, I(’ll| will) go with, let(’s| us) go with,
that works, settled, done, great plan, yes, sure,
happy with, works for me, accept(ed)?, excellent, absolutely

A round passes stage 2 of the pipeline if at least one match is found. Stage 3 additionally scores a numerical disconnect: for each resource mentioned near a quantity in the final turns, the gap between the minimum mentioned number and the total actually submitted is normalized by supply. The composite egregious score is agreement_strength×(1+disconnect)\text{agreement\_strength}\times(1+\text{disconnect}), ranking cases where strong verbal agreement co-occurs with a large numerical divergence between discussed and submitted quantities. 52.3% of all overdrawn rounds pass stage 2 (main 720-game cohort).

Appendix F Additional results

F.1 Targeted prompt interventions

Partial disclosure (Qwen 3.5 Flash ×\times Sonnet 4.5, N=20N{=}20, M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5)

Forcing explicit project disclosure via a system-prompt instruction (Appendix D.1.5) reduced overdraws (28.7% →\rightarrow 17.5%) and improved optimality (20.7% →\rightarrow 28.8%). A parallel Theory-of-Mind elicitation probe (Appendix D.1.5), which asked each agent to reason about the opponent’s likely strategy before submitting, backfired: the optimal rate collapsed to 16.3%, lower than the unaugmented baseline. The ToM prompt appears to introduce over-deliberation, distracting agents from executing their own plans rather than aiding mutual understanding. Together these targeted interventions confirm that simple prompt engineering produces inconsistent gains and cannot substitute for the iterative grounding that emerges from interaction.

Full-transparency intervention (Qwen 3.5 Flash ×\times GPT-5 Mini, N=120N{=}120)

To isolate how much of the coordination gap stems from information asymmetry, we ran a full-transparency intervention in which both agents’ complete project specifications are revealed in the system prompt before cheap talk begins, eliminating information asymmetry entirely. Table 8 shows results across all conditions. Full transparency consistently reduced overdraw and raised efficiency, with the sharpest gains in the stable competitive condition (M/C=0.5M/C{=}0.5: overdraw 11.2%→3.8%11.2\%\to 3.8\%, efficiency 78.1%→89.0%78.1\%\to 89.0\%). However, the optimum rate showed no reliable overall improvement (52.9%→50.0%52.9\%\to 50.0\%) and even declined at M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 (69.4% →\rightarrow 64.4%), confirming that downstream joint planning and execution failures persist even under symmetric complete information.

Table 10 presents self-play performance for additional models, including Qwen 3.6 Plus and MiniMax m2.7, tested on the same negotiation scenarios.

F.2 Token usage by model

Table 11 reports API-reported token counts per agent-round for the three main-cohort models, averaged across all rounds in the 720-game cohort. Completion tokens are further broken down into visible output (speech + action JSON) and thinking (internal chain-of-thought, hidden from the opponent), with all three models spending roughly 70–80% of completion tokens on thinking. Sonnet 4.5 uses far fewer prompt tokens than the other two models due to Anthropic’s prompt caching. Prompt tokens grow across rounds as conversation history accumulates, while completion and thinking tokens decline—agents produce shorter, less deliberative responses as the game progresses.

Appendix I LLM judge: automated behavioral analysis

I.1 Setup

To validate and extend the rule-based failure mode analysis in §5, we ran an automated LLM judge over all 720 game traces. Each game is judged round by round: the judge receives the full cheap-talk transcript, both agents’ allocations, the round outcome, and joint efficiency, then labels every observed behavioral pattern against a canonical taxonomy.

Taxonomy construction.

Patterns are extracted in two steps. In Step 1, the judge LLM (Minimax M2.5) is fed the transcript of a game together with system instructions of the game rules and pre-computed optimal joint allocations. It is instructed to propose up to two labels with annotations per game round. In Step 2, a second LLM call (Gemini 3.1 Pro) consolidates all raw pattern name (2,372 unique strings) to a list of up to 10 positive and 10 negative canonical IDs with a static mapping between raw pattern name and canonical IDs. The final taxonomy contains 8 negative patterns and 8 positive patterns (Tables 12 and 13).

I.2 Pattern prevalence

Tables 12 and 13 report pattern prevalence across all 2,880 rounds (≈\approx48% suboptimal, ≈\approx52% optimal). Negative pattern rates use suboptimal rounds as the denominator; positive pattern rates use optimal rounds. Condition columns report rates within that subgroup using the same denominator convention.

I.3 Alignment with paper failure modes

The four failure modes identified in §5 map cleanly onto the judge taxonomy:

  1. 1.

    Lack of shared interaction history (§5.2) ↔\leftrightarrow Specification Dispute (31.2% of suboptimal rounds). The shifting–stable gap in the judge (34.8% vs. 27.5%, Δ=7.3\Delta{=}7.3 pp) mirrors the efficiency degradation reported in §5.2 (7.7–8.3 pp).

  2. 2.

    Referential binding failures (§5.6) ↔\leftrightarrow Agreement Abandonment (15.2% of suboptimal rounds). Restricting to overdrawn rounds, the rate rises to ≈\approx50%, consistent with the 52.3% verbal-commitment–violation rate identified by the heuristic pipeline. The pattern peaks at M/C=1.0M/C{=}1.0 (18.7%), where verbal agreements are most common.

  3. 3.

    Anchoring and proposal deference (§5.5) ↔\leftrightarrow Defensive Underbidding (17.6% of suboptimal rounds). The judge captures the conservative side of anchoring: agents bid low rather than update. Consistent with the paper’s non-rotating stubborn-anchor finding, Defensive Underbidding is higher in fixed-project games (21.0%) than rotating ones (14.6%).

  4. 4.

    Perfunctory fairness (§5.4) ↔\leftrightarrow Bottleneck Splitting (14.4% of optimal rounds, Table 13). The judge classifies explicit negotiation of the contested resource as a positive coordination strategy, capturing the process rather than the outcome. Its presence in 14.4% of optimal rounds (Table 13)—versus a much lower rate in suboptimal rounds—corroborates the 6.1% perfunctory fairness shortfall reported in §5.4.

I.4 Decomposing rule-based failure buckets

The rule-based classification in §5 leaves two buckets under-explained: No Prior Context (round-1 suboptimal, 160 rounds) and Failed Improvement (rounds 2+ with a changed but still suboptimal allocation, 540 rounds). Table 14 reports the LLM judge’s top negative patterns within each bucket; a round may carry multiple labels so rates do not sum to 100.

The breakdown reveals distinct mechanisms within the two unexplained buckets. No Prior Context is dominated by Specification Dispute (43.1%): in round 1, before any shared history exists, agents immediately disagree about what plan they are pursuing. Failed Improvement shifts toward Defensive Underbidding (25.9%): agents know the prior outcome was suboptimal but negotiate too conservatively rather than renegotiating toward better outcomes. Agreement Abandonment is similarly distributed across both buckets (∼\sim12–16%), consistent with its round-independent character. These judge labels are reflected in the annotations on Figure 6.

Model heterogeneity.

The judge assigns model-specific failure signatures not visible in aggregate statistics. GPT-5 Mini receives a 52.3% Specification Dispute rate in its suboptimal rounds—five times higher than Sonnet 4.5 (10.3%). Sonnet 4.5’s Agreement Abandonment rate (23.7%) is roughly twice that of GPT-5 Mini (12.1%) and Qwen 3.5 Flash (11.7%). These per-model patterns are consistent with the contrasting negotiation personalities described in §5.3.

I.5 Full-transparency pattern comparison

Table 15 compares LLM judge pattern rates between the 120-game baseline and the 120-game full-transparency subset for the Qwen 3.5 Flash ×\times GPT-5 Mini pair. Results are directional only; the judge labels lack a human-annotated ground truth. The transparency alias mappings are derived from a secondary Gemini 3.1 Pro call (see judge/map_transparency_labels.py).

I.6 Canonical examples

For each of the 16 patterns in the taxonomy we provide one representative excerpt drawn from the corpus, pairing the raw trace (cheap-talk speech, private thinking, and final allocation) with the judge’s annotation. Evidence type tags: S = speech (visible to both agents), T = thinking (private scratchpad), A = allocation (final submission).

Negative patterns

Specification Dispute

(game 10a47633, round 1). Each agent enters with a different project definition and treats its own version as ground truth.

[A/T] “According to my game rules, project_c requires stone×\times2, 6 reward.”
[B/T] “My rules show project_c needs gold×\times5, wood×\times1 for 1 reward.”
[A/S] “According to my game rules, project_c requires stone×\times2 and project_b gives 5/run.”
[B/S] “My project_c needs gold×\times5, not stone.”

Judge: Both agents repeatedly asserted incompatible project definitions, with each treating its own rulebook as authoritative rather than seeking collaborative verification. The unresolved dispute caused both to pursue stone-heavy strategies, overshooting supply (11 vs. 10) and annulling the round.

Supply Limit Overshoot

(game 0ae31ef5, round 1). Coordination focused on the wrong resource; allocations collided on an undiscussed one.

[A/S] “Can you avoid buying crystals so we don’t risk annulment?”
[B/S] “I’m considering buying crystals to run project_a three times.”
[A/A] plasma: 6  [B/A] plasma: 4, titanium: 2

Judge: Agents negotiated to avoid crystal overlap but never discussed plasma. Both submitted large plasma requests (total 10 against supply 6), annulling the round. Speech–allocation coherence was absent: the negotiated resource was never the binding constraint.

Defensive Underbidding

(game 5dbb7a88, round 4). Fairness framing leads to under-utilisation of available supply.

[A/S] “Let’s stick with 5 vine each—that’s fair and ensures we both get decent rewards.”
[B/S] “How about 5 vine each?”
[A/A] bamboo: 3, vine: 4  [B/A] amber: 2, vine: 5

Judge: Agents proposed and accepted a 5/5 split of 10-unit vine supply yet together used only 9 units. The fairness anchor prevented either agent from claiming full value; joint efficiency reached only 62%.

Incomplete Coordination

(game 1a400d48, round 3). A flexibility offer is accepted asymmetrically, leaving each side with a different understanding.

[A/S] “If you need more brass I can be flexible (e.g., take 8 copper ++ 4 brass for reward 24).”
[B/S] “If you take 8 copper and 4 brass (reward 24), I could take 6 brass and 3 aether (reward 18).”
[A/A] brass: 4, copper: 8  [B/A] aether: 4, brass: 4

Judge: Agent A took the offered lower allocation as agreed; Agent B did not follow through on its counter-proposal (6 brass + 3 aether), instead submitting 4 brass + 4 aether. Neither allocation matched the negotiated plan, resulting in the lowest-efficiency round (75%) in the game.

Agreement Abandonment

(game 941a713e, round 2). Having detected deception in round 1, Agent A responds with its own misdirection.

[A/T] “They lied to me! They said they’d focus on silicon but bought maximum fiber. I can’t trust them.”
[A/S] “I’m actually leaning toward fiber combinations this round—it seems efficient for my projects.”
[B/S] “I’m thinking quantum paired with silicon could work well for me.”
[A/A] quantum: 3, silicon: 9  [B/A] quantum: 4, silicon: 5

Judge: Agent A’s speech claimed fiber interest while its allocation was silicon-heavy; combined quantum (7) and silicon (14) demands both exceeded supply, producing a dual overdraw. The private thinking trace reveals deliberate misdirection, a clear case of speech–allocation incoherence.

Greedy Monopolization

(game 89fd88e8, round 1). Both agents independently target the same maximum-reward strategy without coordinating.

[A/T] “With $18 I can buy up to 10 coral for $10 and run project_c twice →\rightarrow reward 12.”
[B/T] “My best solo payoff: coral×\times6 ++ trident×\times4, run project_c twice for reward 12.”
[A/A] coral: 5  [B/A] coral: 6, trident: 4

Judge: Both agents pursued the individual maximum independently. Total coral demand (11) exceeded supply (10), causing annulment. Thinking traces confirm each agent computed the optimal solo strategy without modelling joint feasibility.

Communication Refusal

(game 8ac2b9d4, round 3). Agents commit unilaterally to obsidian without waiting for the other to confirm avoidance.

[A/S] “I’ll do that if you avoid obsidian…Could you confirm you’ll avoid obsidian?”
[B/T] “I’ll lock in obsidian-only (9 obsidian →\rightarrow project_b ×\times3).”
[A/A] obsidian: 9  [B/A] obsidian: 9

Judge: Agent A requested explicit confirmation but Agent B unilaterally committed before responding. Both submitted obsidian×\times9 (total 18 against supply 10), annulling the round and breaking the coordination precedent established in rounds 1–2.

Rule Constraint Violation

(game 0bd23214, round 4). The 2-resource-type limit is rediscovered at decision time, forcing abandonment of the negotiated plan.

[B/S] “I’m looking at 1 project_a run (aether×\times3, copper×\times3) and 1 project_b run (brass×\times3).”
[B/T] “Oh no! I can only purchase at most 2 different resource types per round.”
[B/A] brass: 6

Judge: Agent B negotiated a three-resource plan (aether, copper, brass) then discovered the constraint at submission time, reverting to a single-resource fallback that contradicted its stated plan. This was the second consecutive round in which the same agent failed to account for the type limit.

Positive patterns

Explicit Quantity Confirmation

(game 02624f5b, round 1). Presenting labelled options eliminates ambiguity; the selected option is executed faithfully.

[A/S] “I can commit to one of two clean options: (A) I buy only ice…or (B) I buy fur ++ diamond…”
[B/S] “I prefer Option A—you take ice, I’ll avoid it completely.”
[A/A] ice: 10  [B/A] diamond: 2, fur: 8

Judge: Agent A’s option menu forced an unambiguous commit. Both allocations matched stated intentions exactly (A: ice; B: diamond/fur), avoiding supply conflict and achieving the round optimum.

Complementary Partitioning

(game 0226fc2e, round 4). Each agent claims a disjoint resource domain, eliminating all overlap.

[A/S] “I’ll just focus on glass—probably taking all 10 glass.”
[B/S] “I’m planning to take around 5 ruby and pair it with sandstone. Does 5 ruby for me and 1 ruby for you work?”
[A/A] glass: 10  [B/A] ruby: 6

Judge: Perfect resource specialisation: A claimed all glass (10 units), B claimed all ruby (6 units) with zero overlap. Each agent maximised its own reward (24 each) and the joint allocation was fully supply-compatible.

Precedent Replication

(game 086df833, round 2). The successful round-1 split is reproduced without renegotiation.

[A/S] “I’m planning to purchase 6 silicon and 4 quantum for project_a and project_b.”
[B/S] “I’m considering purchasing fiber and quantum for my projects.”
[A/A] quantum: 4, silicon: 6  [B/A] fiber: 6, quantum: 2

Judge: Agent A (with full history) re-proposed the round-1 split; Agent B (fresh context) naturally complemented it. Allocations matched round 1 exactly, confirming stable-mode path dependence used constructively to sustain optimal coordination.

Bottleneck Splitting

(game 247d7bc1, round 3). When no asymmetric agreement can be reached, both agents converge on an equal split of the contested resource.

[A/S] “I agree to 5/5 this round to keep things fair.”
[B/S] “Let’s do 5/5 this round for fairness.”
[A/A] silicon: 5  [B/A] silicon: 5

Judge: After Agent A’s false claim of a rotation agreement was rejected, both agents defaulted to a 5/5 split of 10-unit silicon supply. The symmetric split prevented annulment and captured moderate joint value (A: 10, B: 8 due to differing project efficiencies).

Transparent Disclosure

(game 02624f5b, round 3). Agent B explicitly states a preference with justification, allowing Agent A to commit without guessing.

[A/S] “Option A: I buy 3 diamonds ++ 6 fur…Option B: I buy 3 diamonds ++ 9 ice…”
[B/S] “I strongly prefer Option A—you take 3 diamonds ++ 6 fur. This works perfectly because I’ll buy 9 ice ++ 3 diamonds…”
[A/A] diamond: 3, fur: 6  [B/A] diamond: 3, ice: 9

Judge: B’s explicit preference statement (including the reason) let A lock in Option A immediately. Both allocations matched the agreed split (3++3 diamonds, 6 fur, 9 ice), staying within supply and achieving the round optimum.

Adaptive Accommodation

(game 555aed7e, round 3). Agent B voluntarily accepts a lower payoff to enable Agent A’s high-reward plan.

[A/S] “I’m planning to run project_a 3×3\times and project_b 2×2\times—that needs basalt×\times6 and obsidian×\times9 (cost 18) and yields reward 30.”
[B/S] “I’ll take magma×\times2 ++ basalt×\times4 to run project_a twice (reward 12).”
[A/A] basalt: 6, obsidian: 9  [B/A] basalt: 4, magma: 2

Judge: Agent B conceded the basalt-heavy allocation it could have competed for, accepting reward 12 instead of a potential 16++, to enable A’s reward-30 plan. The asymmetric outcome (30/12) achieved 88% joint efficiency and required no further negotiation.

Constructive Clarification

(game 02624f5b, round 2). A mathematically incorrect counter-proposal is identified and corrected in-dialogue.

[A/S] “I’ll take 8 fur…What do you plan to buy?”
[B/S] “Could we split fur more evenly? If you take 6 fur and I take 4 fur…”
[A/S] “I can’t agree to 6 fur—that only lets me run project_a once…I propose two clean options: A) I take all 6 diamonds…B) I keep my original plan and take 8 fur…”
[B/S] “Both options give me the same reward (8), so I’ll go with Option B—you take 8 fur, I’ll take diamonds.”

Judge: Agent A identified that B’s counter-proposal relied on a miscalculation, re-stated the constraint, and offered clear alternatives. B accepted the corrected plan, and both allocations matched the agreement.

Optimal Efficiency Proposal

(game 5e59d592, round 3). Iterative counter-proposals converge on the round’s highest-efficiency allocation.

[A/S] “Could we adjust to: you take 1 obsidian and 7 basalt, I take 9 obsidian and 3 basalt?”
[B/S] “How about: I’ll take 2 obsidian and 7 basalt, and you take 8 obsidian and 3 basalt.”
[A/A] basalt: 3, obsidian: 8  [B/A] basalt: 7, obsidian: 1

Judge: A proposed an asymmetric split; B counter-proposed a minor adjustment; both honored the final agreement exactly. The resulting allocation achieved 83% joint efficiency—the highest in the game—with perfect supply feasibility.
